preamble: Assibilation of palatalized [dʲ] produces the alveolar affricate [dz]. In Romanian, Latin d was palatalized again before i/e (second palatalization) and became *[dz], preserved in Aromanian and northern Daco-Romanian but simplified to [z] in the standard language. Polish turned Proto-Slavic *ď (from *dj) into dz (*meďa > miedza), Italian has [ddz] from Latin -dj- (medius > mezzo), and Belarusian dzekanne affricates soft /dʲ/ to [dzʲ] (дзень 'day').

examples.note: Second palatalization: d before i palatalized to *[dʲ] and affricated to [dz]; Aromanian keeps dz, standard Romanian later simplified it to z.
Proto-Slavic *ď (< *dj) gives dz in Polish, against ž in Russian (межа) and z in Czech (mez).
Latin -dj- yields either [ddʒ] or [ddz] in Italian; mezzo shows the alveolar outcome.

examples.from: Old East Slavic дьнь 'day' with soft [dʲ]
examples.note: Dzekanne: soft /dʲ/ is regularly realized as the affricate [dzʲ]; the atlas has no separate palatalized-dz symbol.
